Topic Area 2 – Characterization, Logistics, and Rheology of Mixed Plastic Streams Across these studies, a central accomplishment is the demonstration that advanced characterization, dissolution-based recovery, and data-driven analysis can significantly upgrade the quality and usability of recycled plastics. STRAP (Solvent-Targeted Recovery and Precipitation) proved highly effective at recovering near-virgin-quality polymers from multilayer films, preserving molecular weight and eliminating heavy-metal contaminants even from otherwise unrecyclable packaging structures. Complementary rheological analysis confirmed that STRAP-recovered polyethylene maintained shear and extensional behavior matching virgin PE, validating it as a viable, high-performance feedstock for film applications and illustrating its superiority over melt-based reprocessing for complex waste streams. Meanwhile, machine-learning-enabled MIR spectroscopy delivered a practical breakthrough for sorting, achieving near-100% real-time classification accuracy for mixed plastic waste—including dark plastics that evade conventional NIR detection—enabling routing of materials to appropriate upgrading pathways such as STRAP or specialized mechanical reuse streams. In contrast, extensive evaluations of MRF #3–7 streams underscored the heterogeneity and contamination that limit traditional mechanical recycling, demonstrating inconsistent polymer composition and degraded mechanical performance across facilities and seasons. However, mechanical recycling can be strengthened through application-specific sorting and rheology-based quality control, as shown by studies demonstrating that grouping HDPE and PP by prior end-use manufacturing method yields more predictable thermal and mechanical properties suitable for targeted molding processes. Work integrating experimental reprocessing data with CAE simulations further showed that, even as viscosity and crystallization behavior evolve with thermal history, optimized process windows can preserve molding performance; predictive modeling identified temperature and residence time as dominant levers for minimizing degradation and stabilizing recycled PP properties. Taken together, these findings conclude that high-quality, circular plastics systems will rely on hybrid strategies—combining intelligent sorting, dissolution-based recovery for complex films, and data-driven mechanical recycling optimization—to consistently deliver materials that meet performance requirements for demanding applications. Topic Area 3 – Thermal Depolymerization of Mixed Plastic Waste Streams This project demonstrated and compared the thermal degradation of low-quality mixed waste plastics by pyrolysis and thermal oxo-degradation (TOD). Plastic conversion was performed using both lab and pilot scales, and the effect of impurities was quantified. Computational modeling has been developed, and its accuracy has been verified using experimental data. The results not only advance scientific understanding and fill the knowledge gap, but they also provide critical technical insights into developing the commercial reactor and process for plastic waste conversion.
